claim: The DL121 fusion is a synthetic allosteric switch created by inserting the LOV2 domain from A. sativa between residues 120 and 121 of E. coli DHFR.
source: In this fusion, the LOV2 domain of A. sativa is inserted between residues 120 and 121 of the E. coli DHFR βF-βG loop; we refer to this construct as DL121 (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: The text explicitly states the construction of DL121, and Figure 1A,B provides visual confirmation of the domain architecture.

claim: The DL121 fusion displays a twofold increase in DHFR hydride transfer rate (khyd) in response to blue light.
source: The resulting DL121 fusion covalently attaches the N- and C-termini of LOV2 into a sector connected surface on DHFR, and displays a twofold increase in DHFR hydride transfer rate (khyd) in response to blue light (Lee et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work (Lee et al., 2008).

claim: Under steady-state conditions, DL121 exhibits a 28% increase in the turnover number (kcat) in response to light.
source: Under steady-state conditions, we measured a 28% increase in the turnover number (kcat) in response to light and a statistically insignificant change in the Michaelis constant (Km) (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 1C and described in the text.

claim: The change in Michaelis constant (Km) for DL121 in response to light is statistically insignificant.
source: Under steady-state conditions, we measured a 28% increase in the turnover number (kcat) in response to light and a statistically insignificant change in the Michaelis constant (Km) (Figure 1C).
evidence: The text explicitly states the statistical insignificance, supported by data in Figure 1C.

claim: DHFR has no known natural allosteric regulation.
source: As DHFR has no known natural allosteric regulation, the LOV2 insertion confers a new, evolutionarily unoptimized regulatory input.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about DHFR.

claim: When an E. coli DHFR deletion strain complemented with DL121 was grown, the resulting strain grew 17% faster in the light than in the dark.
source: Prior work found that the modest in vitro allosteric effect of DL121 conferred a selectable growth rate advantage in vivo: when an E. coli DHFR deletion strain (ER2566 ΔfolAΔthyA) was complemented with DL121, the resulting strain grew 17% faster in the light than in the dark (Reynolds et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work (Reynolds et al., 2011).

claim: The growth rate assay can discriminate a change of ±0.02 µM−1 s-1 in catalytic power (kcat/Km).
source: More specifically, we can discriminate a change of ±0.02 µM−1 s-1 in catalytic power (kcat/Km) under these conditions.
evidence: This is stated as a measured capability of the assay.

claim: The resolution of the growth-based assay is on par with or better than literature-reported errors for in vitro steady state kinetics measurements of DHFR.
source: This level of precision is on par with – and in some cases better than – literature-reported errors for in vitro steady state kinetics measurements of DHFR (Reynolds et al., 2011; Wagner et al., 1992; Huang et al., 1994).
evidence: The claim compares the assay precision to literature values.

claim: 891 of the 3021 possible missense mutations (29.5%) could not be measured for growth rate.
source: We were unable to measure growth rate for 891 of the 3021 possible missense mutations (19 substitutions over 159 positions): 226 (7.5%) were missing at the start of the experiment (t = 0) for one or more replicates (referred to as 'no data'), and an additional 665 (22%) were depleted from the library before reaching the minimum of three time points required for growth rate estimation (we refer to these as null mutants, see also Materials and methods, Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: The text provides specific counts and percentages of unmeasurable mutations.

claim: The relative growth rates for 2130 mutations (70.5%) were highly reproducible, with a correlation coefficient between replicate pairs above 0.9.
source: The relative growth rates for the remaining 2130 mutations (70.5%) were highly reproducible, with a correlation coefficient between replicate pairs above 0.9 (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The text states the reproducibility metric, supported by Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: Mutations with growth rates at or below the DL121 D27N cutoff were significantly enriched in the sector.
source: We found that mutations with growth rates at or below this cutoff (including the null mutants) were significantly enriched in both the sector (p=7.9×10−8, Figure 3E, Supplementary file 1b) and at evolutionarily conserved positions (p=8.7×10−20, Figure 3—figure supplement 6, Supplementary file 1c).
evidence: The text provides statistical significance values and references figures showing the enrichment.

claim: Mutations with growth rates at or below the DL121 D27N cutoff were significantly enriched at evolutionarily conserved positions.

claim: Positions enriched for deleterious mutations surround the active site and co-factor binding pocket.
source: When mapped to the WT DHFR structure, positions enriched for deleterious mutations surround the active site and co-factor binding pocket (Figure 3F), structurally overlap with the sector (Figure 3G), and include a number of positions known to play a critical role in WT DHFR catalysis (e.g. W22, D27, M42, and L54) (Howell et al., 1986; Fierke et al., 1987).

claim: 1548 mutations representing 51% of the growth assay data were retained for analysis of allostery after removing slow-growing and null mutations.
source: Following the thinking that (near) inactive DHFR variants are both inherently non-allosteric and associated with the least reproducible growth rate measurements (Figure 3—figure supplement 3), we removed the set of 1247 slow-growing (growth rate <−0.13) and null mutations prior to the analysis of allostery. The retained 1548 mutations – representing 51% of the growth assay data – remain well-distributed between the DL121 surface, core, sector, and evolutionarily conserved positions (Figure 3E).
evidence: The text explicitly states the number and percentage of retained mutations.

claim: The choice of LOV2 insertion site was guided by Statistical Coupling Analysis (SCA).
source: The choice of LOV2 insertion site was guided by Statistical Coupling Analysis (SCA), an approach for analyzing coevolution between pairs of amino acids across a homologous protein family (Rivoire et al., 2016; Lockless and Ranganathan, 1999; Halabi et al., 2009).

claim: Co-evolving groups of amino acids, termed sectors, often form physically contiguous networks in the tertiary structure that link allosteric sites to active sites.
source: A central finding of SCA is that co-evolving groups of amino acids, termed sectors, often form physically contiguous networks in the tertiary structure that link allosteric sites to active sites (Halabi et al., 2009; Süel et al., 2003; Pincus et al., 2018).
evidence: The text describes a central finding of SCA, supported by citations.

claim: The DL121 fusion covalently attaches the N- and C-termini of LOV2 into a sector connected surface on DHFR.
source: To create the DL121 fusion, Lee et al. followed the guiding principle that sector connected surface sites in DHFR might serve as preferred sites (or 'hot spots') for the introduction of allosteric regulation (Lee et al., 2008). The resulting DL121 fusion covalently attaches the N- and C-termini of LOV2 into a sector connected surface on DHFR, and displays a twofold increase in DHFR hydride transfer rate (khyd) in response to blue light (Lee et al., 2008).
evidence: The text describes the structural arrangement of the DL121 fusion, supported by citation.

claim: Blue light triggers the formation of a covalent adduct between a cysteine residue (C450) and a flavin mononucleotide (FMN) in LOV2 signaling.
source: In LOV2 signaling, blue light triggers the formation of a covalent adduct between a cysteine residue (C450) and a flavin mononucleotide (FMN, yellow sticks) (Salomon et al., 2001; Crosson and Moffat, 2002; Swartz et al., 2002) and associated unfolding of the C-terminal Jα-helix (red cartoon); this order-to-disorder transition is used for regulation in several synthetic and natural systems (Pudasaini et al., 2015; Glantz et al., 2016).
evidence: The text describes the LOV2 signaling mechanism, supported by multiple citations and Figure 1A.

claim: The order-to-disorder transition of the LOV2 Jα-helix is used for regulation in several synthetic and natural systems.

evidence: The text describes the regulatory mechanism, supported by citations.
